title: Sign Lock-In: Randomly Initialized Weight Signs Persist and Bottleneck Sub-Bit Model Compression
claim: Sign patterns from trained models are nearly incompressible, matching a random i.i.d. baseline, so they impose a fixed one-bit-per-weight floor.
layout: single line plot, rate on x vs distortion bound on y, legend top-right
description: A single matplotlib line plot. The x-axis is Rate in bits per sign, from 0 to about 1.05. The y-axis is the Shannon lower bound on distortion, from 0 to 0.5. A legend in the top right lists four curves with entropy-rate values. Three marked curves are MLP-Mixer-B16 (blue circles, H=0.987), TinyLlama-1.1B-Chat (purple diamonds, H=0.996) and ResNet18 (green squares, H=0.879). A thick black dashed curve is the Rademacher i.i.d. baseline (H=1.000). The blue and purple curves lie almost exactly on the black dashed baseline. They fall convexly from about 0.5 at zero rate to 0 near rate 1. The green ResNet18 curve sits clearly below the others. The eye goes first to the overlapping curves along the dashed baseline, then to the green outlier. Light dotted gridlines run behind the curves.
caption: One-bit wall. Shannon’s rate-distortion lower bound for binary sign patterns under Hamming distortion evaluated using an entropy-rate proxy estimated from pretrained weights. Across all models, this proxy is close to one, and the bound is nearly indistinguishable from that of an i.i.d. Rademacher baseline, indicating that sign patterns contain little redundancy.
abstract: Sub-bit model compression targets storage below one bit per weight; as magnitudes are aggressively compressed, the sign bit becomes a fixed-cost bottleneck. Across Transformers, CNNs, and MLPs, learned sign matrices resist low-rank approximation and are spectrally indistinguishable from an i.i.d. Rademacher baseline. This randomness gives rise to the lower bound of sub-bit model compression -- the one-bit wall. Despite this apparent randomness, most weights retain their initialization signs; flips primarily occur via rare near-zero boundary crossings, suggesting that sign-pattern randomness is largely inherited from initialization. We formalize this behavior with sign lock-in theory, a stopping-time analysis of sign flips under SGD noise. Under bounded updates and a rare re-entry condition into a small neighborhood of zero, the number of effective sign flips exhibits a geometric tail. Building on this mechanism, we introduce a from-scratch low-rank sign-template training method that prevents the emergence of this one-bit wall.
